chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Ahmad bin Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Ammar bin Marwan, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the fraud (al-ghulul). He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever is defrauded from the Imam (peace be upon him) is ill-gotten gain (suh't), and consuming the wealth of the orphan and its like is ill-gotten gain. And ill-gotten gains are of many types; among them are the payments for the immoralities, and the price of wine and the intoxicating nabidh, and usury after the proof. So as for the bribe in judgment, then that is disbelief in Allah the Magnificent and in His Messenger (peace be upon him and his family).'

key_terms.أُجُورُ الْفَوَاجِرِ: Payments for those who commit immoralities (prostitution)
key_terms.النَّبِيذِ الْمُسْكِرِ: Intoxicating nabidh (a type of fermented drink)
key_terms.الْغُلُولِ: Fraud or embezzlement, specifically of war booty or public funds

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on bribery in judgment and how does it relate to the Imam's wealth?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that 'al-ghulul' specifically refers to embezzlement from the Imam, categorizing it as 'suh't' (ill-gotten gain) akin to consuming an orphan's wealth. The hadith further enumerates common sources of suh't, such as usury and prices of intoxicants, while elevating bribery in judicial rulings to the status of major disbelief (kufr), reflecting the Shia emphasis on the Imam's authority in economic and legal matters.
